core: Typographic hierarchy: organizing text into levels of importance (title/headline, subhead, body, caption, and labels) so readers can navigate and scan, each level given a distinct type treatment
The variables that signal a level with type: size, weight, style (roman/italic, all caps, small caps), color/value, case, and spacing (leading and space-before/after)
That hierarchy is more than making headings bigger: it uses contrast, proximity, and repetition to organize information and reduce cognitive load

The type scale and the modular scale: an ordered set of sizes linked by a common ratio, so each step is proportionally larger; the classic Bringhurst scale (~6-72 pt) and common ratios (major third 1.25, perfect fifth 1.5, golden section ~1.618)

Font/type pairing: combining typefaces for contrast plus harmony; a reliable approach pairs a serif with a sans (classification contrast) or two weights/styles of one family; superfamilies; limiting to about two to three typefaces; avoiding near-identical pairings
supporting: Choosing type by role: a text/body typeface should have a moderate-to-large x-height, low-to-moderate stroke contrast, distinguishable letterforms, and open counters; a display typeface (headlines) has more room to be expressive
How many heading levels a design needs, and whether emphasis is needed inside body copy, are practical requirements that drive the number of levels
Scanning behavior (readers skim rather than read every word) is the reason a clear hierarchy improves usability
outOfScope: General visual hierarchy across any page element using size, position, color, and whitespace (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:visual-hierarchy); referenced, not re-taught
Type anatomy and the definitions of kerning, tracking, and leading (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:typography-basics); referenced, not re-taught
The serif/sans-serif/script/slab classification categories themselves (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:typeface-classification); named here only as a contrast device
Web/CSS type mechanics (rem/em, responsive type, variable fonts) and licensing of specific fonts

claims.claim: Typographic hierarchy organizes text into levels of importance-such as headings, subheadings, and body text, with captions, quotes, callouts, and footnotes in secondary or tertiary positions-each given distinct type styling so readers can navigate content by importance.
Hierarchy is not solely about making headings bigger; it uses contrast, proximity, and repetition to visually organize information, which improves usability and reduces cognitive load.

Headings are typically the largest and often boldest text, signaling primary topics; subheadings are slightly smaller and less prominent; body text forms the bulk of content and is optimized for readability. Size and weight are therefore primary signals of a text level.

A typographic scale is an ordered set of sizes linked by a common ratio: if a size f is in the scale then r*f is also in the scale, so each size is proportionally larger than the last, analogous to notes in a musical scale. The classic scale documented by Robert Bringhurst runs roughly 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21, 24, 30, 36, 48, 60, 72 points.

A modular scale generates sizes by multiplying a base size by a fixed ratio; commonly used ratios include the major third (1.25), the perfect fifth (1.5), and the golden section (about 1.618), several of which are borrowed from musical intervals.

Font pairing works by combining contrast with harmony: successful pairings combine thick with thin, ornate with simple, or sans serif with serif, while two typefaces that are almost-but-not-quite alike are 'too close for comfort' and clash. Pairing a serif with a sans is a reliable strategy because the classification difference supplies instant contrast.

Harmony can also come from staying within one family: different weights (regular and bold) of a single typeface create hierarchy without adding a new typeface, and superfamilies are designed to pair. Most projects need only about two to three typefaces.
Two typefaces that do not work well together at the same point size may pair well at contrasting sizes, so pairing decisions and hierarchy both depend on thoughtful sizing.

When selecting type by role, an effective text (body) typeface should have a moderate-to-large x-height, low-to-moderate contrast, distinguishable letterforms, and open counters; a display typeface, used for headlines and large sizes, can be more expressive. Practical requirements include how many heading levels are required and whether emphasis is needed within body copy.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether modular scales must use one exact mathematical ratio.
positions: Purely geometric view: every size is the previous size times a constant ratio r, giving a clean progression.

Historical/practical view: the classic 400-year-old typographic scale documented by Bringhurst is not perfectly geometric-it packs more sizes at the small end and contains human 'errors' (for example the 11 pt size does not fit a strict ratio), because metal sizes were chosen for practical use.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the modular scale as the underlying idea (a base size times a consistent ratio) and notes that real-world scales, including the classic one, bend the math for practical reasons rather than following a single ratio slavishly.

sourceRecords.title: How to Pair Fonts: A Practical Guide
sourceRecords.notes: Practical font-pairing guide by Mia Cinelli. Supports: pairings combine contrast (thick with thin, ornate with simple, sans serif with serif) with harmony; near-identical pairings are 'too close for comfort' (crediting Ellen Lupton) and clash; within one family, bold and regular weights create hierarchy without a new typeface; two to three typefaces are usually sufficient; and two typefaces that clash at the same point size may pair well at contrasting sizes. sourceRecords.title: The Typographic Scale
sourceRecords.notes: Technical article on the typographic scale. Defines the scale as an ordered set of sizes in visual harmony where, if f is a size in the scale, r*f is also in the scale (r is the scale ratio), giving a geometric progression analogous to a musical scale. Documents the classic scale attributed to Robert Bringhurst's The Elements of Typographic Style (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21, 24, 30, 36, 48, 60, 72 pt) and notes the historical scale is not perfectly geometric. Fetched 2026-08-19. Marked '(c) 2011, all rights reserved'; treated as reference only for these well-established facts, with no wording reproduced.
